rationale: B wins because it is tighter: three real shapes, no padded fourth, and the proof questions are sharper where the story could collapse. A's strongest line, "An unprofitable automaker just turned its charging network into a revenue line," is excellent, but its "Rivian just bet that an exclusive charging network isn't worth keeping" leans on an industry-moat thesis the supplied facts do not prove. B's "Rivian adds Tesla-style plugs and opens its network with no automaker partner in sight" keeps the infrastructure story closer to the evidence and tells the founder exactly what must be verified before pitching.
gaps_in_A: "The prevailing belief: a proprietary fast-charging network is a moat" imports an industry premise not supplied in the update; usable as a thesis only after outside reporting, not as a grounded angle here.

"what it says about the moat thesis the rest of the industry still holds" is too broad for the evidence. The update proves Rivian opened access; it does not prove what the rest of the industry believes.
Four kept angles is defensible, but the contrarian angle partially overlaps with the revenue/utilization angle; it needs harder proof before it earns its own lane.
gaps_in_B: "whether opening the network dilutes a perk existing owners bought into" is a fair question, but the update does not say Rivian marketed the network as an owner-exclusive perk; keep it as proof-needed, not a pitch claim.
"with no automaker partner in sight" pushes past "no partnership announced." Fine for a headline draft, but a reporter will hear certainty that the facts do not yet support.
"counterposition" is jargon. The angle itself works; the label sounds like someone naming a strategy deck tab.
